It reuses intermediate results stored in the forward pass
It only updates the last layer, so far less is computed
It skips most of the weights, which have zero gradient

distractors: It needs the forward pass's stored values.

mcq.q: Why do hard negatives help most?
options: They are easy to label by hand, so data is cheap
Similar but wrong, so they teach fine distinctions
They are random, so they cover more topics per batch
They make each training step run faster on a GPU
mcq.why: Random negatives are too easy; near-misses teach the boundaries that matter.
distractors: Ease of labelling is not why they help.
Random negatives are usually easy and teach little.
They make learning more effective, not faster.

mcq.q: How does the InfoNCE loss treat training?
options: Softmax over similarities, positive as the class
As clustering of queries and passages
As regression on the distances
As reinforcement learning with rewards
mcq.why: The positive passage should get the highest similarity among all candidates.
distractors: InfoNCE is a classification loss.
It does not predict distances.
There are no actions or rewards.

mcq.q: What is the difference between token embeddings and sentence embeddings?
options: Token embeddings are what you store for RAG search, sentence ones are internal
Token embeddings: an LLM's input table; sentence embeddings: a separate model, for the vector DB
Sentence embeddings are the first layer of every LLM, one per vocabulary entry
They are the same vectors, just computed for texts of different lengths
mcq.why: They are easy to confuse; RAG uses sentence or passage embeddings (chapter 9).
distractors: It is the other way round: sentence embeddings go in the vector database.
That describes token embeddings.
They come from different models and serve different jobs.

mcq.q: A general embedding model places “PTO” far from “annual leave”. What does the topic suggest?
options: Remove acronyms from the documents before indexing
Use a larger LLM to write the answers
Switch to keyword search only, without embeddings
Evaluate on your terms; domain-tune the model if needed
mcq.why: General models may never have seen internal acronyms; domain tuning teaches them.
distractors: Acronyms are what users type; removing them loses meaning.
The failure is in retrieval, before the LLM.
Keyword search misses paraphrases; measure and tune instead.

mcq.q: You use an LLM's internal hidden states as search embeddings without evaluating them. What is the risk?
options: They are too small to separate documents
They cannot be stored in a vector database
General hidden states are not retrieval vectors
They are always better than embedding models
mcq.why: Embedding models are trained specifically for similarity; measure before you rely on anything else.
distractors: Size is not the issue; they were not trained for retrieval.
They can; they just may not retrieve well.
Nothing guarantees that; evaluate first.

mcq.q: Which tasks exploit embedding similarity? Choose all that apply.
options: Clustering
Exact arithmetic on amounts
Deduplication
Retrieval
mcq.why: Nearby vectors mean similar text, which powers search, grouping, duplicate detection and routing.
distractors: Arithmetic needs exact computation, not similarity.

mcq.q: A team stores an LLM's token-embedding rows, averaged per document, in a vector database for RAG, and retrieval is poor. What is the most likely mistake?
options: The vectors were not normalised, which is the only reason retrieval fails
They used the input lookup table instead of a sentence embedding model
The vector database needs more dimensions than the LLM provides
Token embeddings work only for English, so other text was lost
mcq.why: Token embeddings are an LLM's per-token lookup; RAG needs vectors from an embedding model trained to put matching texts close together.
distractors: Normalisation matters for scoring, but averaged token rows were never trained for retrieval.
Dimension count is not the problem; the training objective is.
The issue is what the vectors were trained for, not language.

mcq.q: An embedding model ranks “How do I reset my 2FA?” closest to a passage about resetting passwords, not the 2FA guide. You have query–passage pairs. Which training change helps most?
options: Train it to predict the next token of each passage instead
Fine-tune with only random passages from other topics as negatives
Add more dimensions to the vectors without changing the training data
Fine-tune contrastively with similar-but-wrong passages as hard negatives
mcq.why: Hard negatives teach exactly the fine distinction the model is missing.
distractors: Next-token training does not teach query–passage matching.
Random negatives are easy and teach little about close confusions.
Size does not teach the missing distinction.

mcq.q: How does a CNN process an image?
options: It sorts the pixels by brightness first
It slides small learned filters to detect local patterns
It attends from every pixel to every other pixel
It reads the pixels one at a time with a hidden state
mcq.why: Filters detect edges, then textures, parts and objects in deeper layers.
distractors: CNNs keep the spatial layout.
That describes attention, not convolution.
That describes an RNN.

mcq.q: Why are CNNs efficient?
options: They look at only one pixel at a time
They have no weights to learn
Filter weights are shared across positions
They skip training and use fixed filters
mcq.why: Weight sharing means far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer over the image.
distractors: Filters cover small regions, not single pixels.
The filters are learned weights.
The filters are trained.

mcq.q: A 3×3 filter slides over a 6×6 image with stride 1 and no padding. What is the output size?
mcq.why: Output width = 6 − 3 + 1 = 4 in each direction.
distractors: That is the filter size.
That would need a larger filter or stride.
That needs padding.

mcq.q: In an RNN, which weights are applied at each time step?
options: No weights; it only carries state
The same weights at every step
New weights for every step
Only the output layer's weights
mcq.why: hₜ = f(W·xₜ + U·hₜ₋₁) reuses W and U along the sequence.
distractors: The step uses learned weights.
Weights are shared across time.
The hidden-state update uses weights at every step.

mcq.q: Why does information from early tokens fade in an RNN?
options: It must survive many hidden-state updates
Early tokens are read only once, at the start
The vocabulary is too small to hold them
RNNs delete old tokens after a fixed window
mcq.why: Repeated multiplication shrinks the signal over long spans.
distractors: Every token is read exactly once; the problem is how its information is carried.
Vocabulary size does not cause fading.
Nothing is deleted; it fades through repeated multiplication.

mcq.q: Which gates does an LSTM use?
options: Mean and variance
Query, key and value
Encoder and decoder
Forget, input and output
mcq.why: Gates learn what to keep, write and expose from the cell state.
distractors: Those are normalisation statistics.
Those are attention's projections.
Those are seq2seq components.

mcq.q: What was the bottleneck in RNN sequence-to-sequence models?
options: They could not be trained at all
The input had to fit one fixed vector
Outputs were limited to one word
The decoder had no learned weights
mcq.why: A single vector must carry everything about a long input.
distractors: They trained; long inputs were the problem.
Decoders produced whole sequences.
The decoder was a trained RNN.

mcq.q: How did attention fix the seq2seq bottleneck?
options: By removing the encoder and decoding the input directly
By training only on shorter inputs that fit the vector
The decoder weights every encoder state directly
By using a bigger fixed vector between the two networks
mcq.why: Generating “student” can focus on “étudiant”, whatever the input length.
distractors: Attention needs the encoder's states.
That avoids the problem instead of fixing it.
Any fixed vector still limits long inputs.

mcq.q: Why can an RNN not be parallelised across time during training?
options: Sequences must be sorted by length first
RNNs have too few parameters to split
Each step needs the previous step's hidden state
GPUs cannot run recurrent networks
mcq.why: The strict left-to-right dependency forces sequential computation.
distractors: Sorting is an efficiency trick, not the reason.
Parameter count is not the issue.
GPUs run RNNs, just with little parallelism.

mcq.q: Where do CNN-based models still commonly appear in document pipelines?
options: Layout detection and OCR, before the LLM
Storing vectors for semantic search
Choosing the next token in the LLM
Rate limiting requests to the API
mcq.why: Detecting tables and reading scanned text are vision tasks (10.3).
distractors: Vector stores hold embeddings; CNNs are not involved.
That is the language model's decoding.
Rate limiting is infrastructure, not a model.

mcq.q: An RNN's hidden state multiplies early-token information by about 0.9 at each step. Roughly how much survives after 50 tokens?
options: About 90%
About 0.5%
About 45%
About 10%
mcq.why: 0.9⁵⁰ ≈ 0.005: repeated multiplication makes early information fade, which is the RNN limitation.
distractors: The factor applies at every step, not once.
That is 50 × 0.9 ÷ 100, which adds instead of multiplying.
That is one step's loss read as the total.

mcq.q: A seq2seq translator built from two RNNs translates short sentences well but drops details from long paragraphs. Which change addresses the cause?
options: Double the size of the fixed vector between encoder and decoder
Add attention so the decoder can weight every encoder state directly
Replace the decoder RNN with a CNN over the output words
Shorten the paragraphs before translating them
mcq.why: The fixed vector is a bottleneck for long inputs; attention lets each output look back at the relevant positions.
distractors: Any fixed vector still limits long inputs.
The bottleneck is between encoder and decoder, not the decoder type.
That avoids the bottleneck instead of fixing it.
